lessons.title: Why macadamia trees need water and how the system works
lessons.html:
Water and the macadamia tree

Macadamia trees need water to grow, to flower and to fill their nuts. If the tree is too dry when the nuts are growing, the nuts stay small and the kernel is poor. Too much water is also bad. Wet soil for a long time can make the roots rot.

In many parts of Mpumalanga, Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal, rain does not fall at the right time. So the farm gives extra water. This is called irrigation.

Parts of the irrigation system

  • Water source – a dam, borehole or river. The farm must use water legally, under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.
  • Pump – pushes the water into the pipes.
  • Filters – catch sand and dirt so the drippers do not block.
  • Main line and sub-mains – big pipes that carry water to each block.
  • Valves – open and close water to a block.
  • Laterals – the small pipes along each row.
  • Drippers or micro-sprinklers – give water to each tree.

The irrigation schedule

The farm manager decides when each block gets water and for how long. This plan is the schedule. It is based on the weather, the soil, the age of the trees and readings from soil moisture probes. Your job is to follow the schedule exactly.

Stay safe

  • Only switch pumps on or off if you have been trained and told to.
  • Keep away from electrical boxes. Never open them. Report any loose wire or sparks at once.
  • Do not drink water from the irrigation lines. Fertiliser may be in it.
  • Be careful around dams. Never swim in a farm dam.

lessons.title: Running and checking the irrigation
lessons.html:
Doing the irrigation work

Before you start, get the schedule from your supervisor. It tells you which blocks to water, in what order and for how long.

Opening a block

  1. Check that the pump is running, or ask the person in charge of the pump.
  2. Open the valve for the correct block slowly. Opening or closing valves fast can make a water hammer that bursts pipes.
  3. Write down the start time.
  4. When the time is up, close the valve slowly and write down the end time.

Walking the lines

While the block is running, walk the rows and look and listen. Look for:

  • Leaks – water spraying from a pipe or a joint.
  • Blocked drippers – a dry spot where a dripper should be wet.
  • Broken or missing micro-sprinklers.
  • Pools of water – too much water in one place.
  • Pipes cut by a slasher, a bakkie or animals like porcupines and moles.

Fix small problems if you are trained to, for example putting a missing dripper back. Mark big problems with a flag or tape and report them to your supervisor the same day.

Cleaning filters

Dirty filters slow the water down. Clean them as your supervisor shows you. Close the water before you open a filter. Rinse the screen or discs and put them back correctly.

Records

Write down in the irrigation book or on the app: date, block, start time, end time, problems found and what you did. Good records help the manager see if the trees are getting enough water.

Key points

  • Too little water gives small nuts; too much can rot the roots.
  • Follow the irrigation schedule exactly.
  • Open and close valves slowly.
  • Walk the lines and report leaks and blocked drippers.
  • Record every irrigation and never touch electrical boxes.
